title: Charles Sumner Bunn
summary: Charles Sumner Bunn (1865–1952) was a Shinnecock decoy carver, guide, church elder, trustee, and historical witness whose public life joined creative work, community governance, and land memory.
content:
Charles Sumner Bunn (1865–1952) was a Shinnecock decoy carver, hunting and boating guide, church elder, trustee, and historical witness. His life connects creative work on Shinnecock Bay with community governance, a 1935 effort to secure voting rights for Shinnecock women, and testimony about reservation boundaries and community memory.1

Family and community memory

Bunn was the son of David Waukus Bunn and Mary Emma Cuffee Bunn. His father, a whaler, died during the December 1876 Circassian rescue effort when Charles was a child. Charles later carried family and community knowledge into his own work and public testimony. His daughter Alice Osceola Bunn Martinez became an important source for the detailed account of his carving and guiding reproduced in Stone’s community history.2

Carving, guiding, and life on the water

Bunn made his living through guiding and decoy carving. Alice Bunn Martinez recalled him packing barrels of locally shaped bird decoys for the annual sportsmen’s show in New York City and returning without unsold work. John A. Strong describes Bunn and Eugene Cuffee as highly skilled decoy carvers and reproduces a circa-1920 photograph of Bunn with his display. Bunn also guided visiting hunters and took boating parties onto local waters in his catboat, the Dore E.3

Trustee and church service

Records reproduced by Stone show Bunn elected repeatedly as a Shinnecock trustee between 1890 and 1942. In April 1900, Bunn and fellow trustees John H. Thompson and Arthur Carll renewed an agreement governing art students’ access to paint on the reservation and use the Sailboat Dock. Jensen also identifies Bunn as an elder of the Shinnecock Presbyterian Church. These roles place his artistic life alongside long service in community institutions.4

The 1935 voting-rights motion

At the annual meeting of adult Shinnecock members at Southampton Town Hall on April 2, 1935, Bunn attended as a tribal member rather than as one of the three trustees elected that day. He moved that Assemblyman John Downs be asked to introduce legislation allowing Shinnecock women to vote at the annual meeting; David Kellis seconded the motion. The request did not produce voting rights then. Shinnecock women secured the franchise decades later, following sustained organizing within the community.5

Testimony about the reservation boundary

In 1952, at age eighty-six, Bunn testified in the King reservation-boundary litigation. Stone’s account says he shared traditions learned from earlier community members and testified that a Shinnecock church once stood on the disputed strip before 1859 and had been moved away during the night. The testimony shows an elder using remembered community history in a legal struggle over land, while the surviving account remains a later published description of his court appearance rather than a full transcript of his words.6

A photographed community gathering

A circa-1934 photograph at Conscience Point places Bunn with Eugene Cuffee, Charles Martinez, Elliot Kellis, Alice Bunn Martinez, David Martinez, Anthony Beaman, and Marjorie Martinez. The caption documents a community gathering and helps connect Bunn’s public record to named Shinnecock relatives and contemporaries without assigning roles that the photograph does not state.7

Reading the map

The map chronology connects broad or public places associated with Bunn’s documented work: Shinnecock, the New York sportsmen’s show, Southampton Town Hall, and the Riverhead courthouse. The line orders those records by date; it is not a reconstruction of his exact travel route.

References

  • Beverly Jensen, Shinnecock Indian Nation (2015), p. 30.
  • Gaynell Stone, ed., The Shinnecock Indians: A Culture History, vol. VI (1983), pp. 130, 162–163, 178, 182, 185, 190–191, 199, 208, 297–298, 351, and 380.
  • John A. Strong, The Algonquian Peoples of Long Island from Earliest Times to 1700 (1997), p. 269.
  • David Bunn Martine, Shinnecock History Timeline, p. 11.
why_this_matters: Charles Sumner Bunn’s life brings artistic labor, community leadership, and legal memory into one story. His decoys and guiding work supported a household, while his trustee service, 1935 voting-rights motion, and later boundary testimony show how cultural knowledge and civic action remained connected across generations.
activity_update_summary: Added a source-supported biography of Shinnecock carver and guide Charles Sumner Bunn with four linked Historic Moments, a public-location chronology, trustee and church service, the 1935 voting-rights motion, and his 1952 boundary testimony.
